_meta.purpose: Curated STRIDE threat rules for iac-tools:threat-model. Each rule matches a semantic node kind (from graph_semantics.TYPE_MAP) and attribute conditions, and names the Checkov rules whose PASS marks the threat mitigated.
governance: STATIC, CHECKED-IN, HUMAN-REVIEWED DATA. The model never adds, removes, or re-scores a rule at runtime.
Every id in `mitigations` MUST exist in security-scan/data/rule-severity.json or security-scan/data/control-map.json. tests/test_threat_rules.py enforces this.

NIST 800-53 control IDs reach a threat by exactly two routes: (1) a Checkov id in `mitigations` that control-map.json maps, or (2) an explicit `nist_800_53` list on the rule that carries `source: "curated"` and a written `rationale`, and whose IDs already appear in the checked-in control vocabulary. Anything else is dropped and logged. When in doubt, cite none.
A rule with `mitigations: []` describes a weakness no Checkov check can offset. With Checkov data present it reports `unmitigated`; without Checkov data every threat reports `unknown`.
`threat` text is a statement about the architecture, not about the IaC author. Names from the IaC are untrusted and are only ever substituted into the {id} placeholder.

conditionGrammar.kinds: list of semantic kinds, or ["*"] for any kind
conditionGrammar.when: object; every entry must hold. key = dotted path into the node (`kind`, `type`, `flags.x`). value = literal (equality; null means missing) or an operator object: eq, ne, in, not_in, exists, nonempty, gte, lte, lt, gt, contains, any_in
conditionGrammar.when_any: optional list of `when` objects; at least one must hold in addition to `when`
conditionGrammar.evidence: flag paths copied into the threat so the reader sees why it fired
conditionGrammar.evidenceAddresses: flag paths holding resource addresses that also count when matching Checkov results (an SG rule resource, a listener)

reviewed.note: Curated 2026-10-06 for threat-model v1. The four curated nist_800_53 entries reuse the control that control-map.json assigns to the sibling Checkov concept; each rationale names that sibling.

rules.title: Internet-facing load balancer without a WAF
rules.threat: {id} accepts traffic from any internet address with no web application firewall in front of it. An attacker can flood it or probe the application behind it without any request filtering.

rules.title: Public load balancer accepts plain HTTP
rules.threat: {id} has an HTTP listener that forwards traffic instead of redirecting to HTTPS. Credentials and session data cross the internet in clear text and can be read or altered in transit.

rules.title: Load balancer without access logs
rules.threat: {id} does not write access logs. Requests that reach the application leave no record, so an attack cannot be reconstructed or attributed afterwards.

rules.title: Administrative port open to the internet
rules.threat: {id} allows SSH, RDP, or WinRM from any internet address. Password guessing and credential replay against the attached hosts need no foothold inside the network.

rules.title: Database port open to the internet
rules.threat: {id} allows a database or cache port from any internet address. The data store behind it is one credential away from direct read and write access.
rules.rationale: Network-level public exposure of a data port. control-map.json assigns SC-7 (boundary protection) to the sibling port-specific checks CKV_AWS_24, CKV_AWS_25 and CKV_AWS_277; Checkov has no check for database ports, so the same control is applied by analogy.

rules.title: All ports open to the internet
rules.threat: {id} allows every port and protocol from any internet address. Every service on the attached hosts is reachable, including ones that were never meant to be exposed.

rules.title: Internet ingress on a non-web port
rules.threat: {id} allows internet traffic on ports other than 80 and 443. Services on those ports are usually not hardened for public exposure.

rules.title: Subnet assigns public IP addresses by default
rules.threat: Every instance launched into {id} receives a public IP address unless the launch overrides it. Resources become internet-reachable by default rather than by decision.

rules.title: Compute with a public IP address
rules.threat: {id} is reachable directly from the internet instead of through a load balancer. Its security group is the only control between an attacker and the host.

rules.title: VPC without flow logs
rules.threat: {id} does not record network flows. Lateral movement and data exfiltration inside the VPC leave no trace.

rules.title: Public API without a WAF
rules.threat: {id} is a public API with no web application firewall. Request floods and injection probes reach the backend unfiltered.

rules.title: API stage without access logging
rules.threat: {id} does not log API requests. Abuse of the API cannot be detected or reconstructed.

rules.title: API method without authorization
rules.threat: {id} exposes methods with authorization NONE. Anyone can call them as if they were a legitimate client.

rules.title: CloudFront serves over plain HTTP
rules.threat: {id} allows viewers to connect over HTTP. Content and cookies can be read or altered on the path to the viewer.

rules.title: CloudFront without a WAF
rules.threat: {id} has no web ACL. Request floods and injection probes pass through to the origin.

rules.title: Publicly accessible database
rules.threat: {id} is configured as publicly accessible. If its security group or subnet routing ever opens, the database is directly on the internet.

rules.title: Public S3 bucket
rules.threat: {id} grants access to everyone through its ACL or bucket policy, and no public access block stops it. Its objects can be listed, read, or written from the internet.

rules.title: Database storage not encrypted at rest
rules.threat: {id} stores data without encryption at rest. Snapshots, backups, and the underlying volumes expose the data in clear text to anyone who obtains them.

rules.title: DynamoDB table without a customer managed key
rules.threat: {id} relies on the AWS owned key. Access to the data cannot be revoked or audited through a key policy.

rules.title: S3 bucket without server-side encryption
rules.threat: {id} has no default encryption configuration declared. Objects written without an explicit encryption header are stored in clear text.

rules.title: EFS file system not encrypted
rules.threat: {id} stores files without encryption at rest. Backups and the storage layer expose file contents in clear text.
rules.rationale: Encryption of data at rest. control-map.json assigns SC-28 to the sibling at-rest checks CKV_AWS_16 (RDS) and CKV_AWS_19 (S3); the EFS check CKV_AWS_42 is not in the map, so the same control is applied by analogy.

rules.title: Database without deletion protection
rules.threat: {id} can be deleted by a single API call. A compromised deployer credential or a mistaken apply destroys the data store.

rules.title: Database without log exports
rules.threat: {id} does not export its engine logs. Failed logins and slow or unusual queries are not available for detection.

rules.title: S3 bucket without access logging
rules.threat: {id} does not log object access. Bulk downloads cannot be detected or proven after the fact.

rules.title: Public database snapshot
rules.threat: {id} is shared with every AWS account. Anyone can restore it and read the full database.

rules.title: KMS key policy with a wildcard principal
rules.threat: The key policy of {id} grants a statement to every principal without a condition. Anyone who can reach the key can use or administer it.

rules.title: Policy allows every action
rules.threat: {id} grants Action "*". Whoever holds the attached identity can perform any operation the resource list allows, including changing permissions.

rules.title: Full administrative access
rules.threat: {id} carries "*" on "*" or the AdministratorAccess policy. Compromise of the identity is compromise of the account.

rules.title: Service-wide wildcard action
rules.threat: {id} grants every action of a service (for example dynamodb:*). A read-only workload can delete tables, change encryption, or export data. No Checkov check detects a service-scoped wildcard.
rules.rationale: Least privilege. control-map.json assigns AC-6 to the sibling wildcard checks CKV_AWS_63 (Action *) and CKV_AWS_355 (Resource *); a service-scoped wildcard is the same concept at a narrower scope and has no Checkov check, so the same control is applied by analogy.

rules.title: Wildcard resource
rules.threat: {id} grants actions on Resource "*". The identity can act on every resource of that service in the account, not only the ones this stack owns.

rules.title: Privilege escalation actions
rules.threat: {id} grants actions that can be used to gain more privilege (PassRole, policy versioning, attaching policies, AssumeRole). The identity can become a more powerful one.

rules.title: Role assumable by anyone
rules.threat: The trust policy of {id} names Principal "*". Any AWS account can assume this role and act with its permissions.

rules.title: External or federated trust without a condition
rules.threat: {id} trusts another account or an identity provider with no Condition on the statement. Any identity that principal vouches for can assume the role; a confused-deputy or audience mismatch becomes a login.

rules.title: IMDSv1 allowed
rules.threat: {id} does not require IMDSv2. A server-side request forgery in the application can read the instance role credentials from the metadata service and use them from anywhere.

rules.title: Secret stored in a plain attribute
rules.threat: {id} carries a credential as a literal value. It is in version control, in the plan output, and in the state file; anyone with read access to any of them holds the secret.
rules.rationale: Authenticator management. control-map.json assigns IA-5 to the hardcoded-secret checks CKV_AWS_41, CKV_AWS_45 and CKV_AWS_46. Those checks are not cited as mitigations here because CKV_AWS_45 passes on tf-02's Lambda while three literal secrets remain in its environment (answer-key TF-02-5); a pass must not flip a structurally present secret to mitigated.

rules.title: EBS volume explicitly not encrypted
rules.threat: {id} declares a block device with encryption off. Snapshots of the volume expose its contents in clear text.

rules.title: Lambda environment not encrypted with a customer key
rules.threat: {id} stores environment variables under the default key. Anyone with lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration reads them; a customer key would require kms:Decrypt as well.

rules.title: Lambda invokable by anyone
rules.threat: {id} can be invoked from the internet without authentication, through a function URL with no auth or a permission granted to Principal "*".

rules.title: Privileged container
rules.threat: A container in {id} runs privileged. Escape from the container to the host is trivial.

rules.title: Log group retention under one year
rules.threat: {id} discards logs in under a year. Evidence of an intrusion discovered late is already gone.
